e.t: Adramelech is a proper name, rendered as “Adramelech” or “Athramelekh.” It identifies a particular person or figure rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs three times: twice in 2 Kings and once in Isaiah. The name itself does not provide a broader ordinary meaning beyond identifying its bearer. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and account.

Aer is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:12. Because the available information identifies only the name and its occurrence, it does not establish an additional descriptive meaning or explain the person’s role in that passage. The surrounding verse and genealogical context are needed to understand how Aer is presented there.

This word means “age” or “-ever”. As a noun, it refers to a span or continuation of time, and in English it may be rendered “ever” when the sense emphasizes enduring duration. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 541 times, showing that this is a widely used word for time across the LXX corpus. It does not by itself explain the specific force of every passage; surrounding words determine whether the emphasis falls on an age or on continuity through time.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Alleli” or “Allili.” It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 26:22. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as a personal designation. The two supplied renderings represent the same name in English transliteration, not separate meanings.

This Greek LXX verb means “sin”: to do what is morally wrong before God. It describes wrongdoing as an action, rather than merely naming a sinful condition. The word appears 234 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, showing that it is used broadly for human failure and disobedience. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This adverb means “without reward,” describing an action done without receiving payment or compensation. It points to the absence of expected return rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 24:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the same: something is done without reward.

Forgivingness means the quality or practice of being forgiving. As a noun, it names an attitude or disposition rather than an action word. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:21. The word’s central idea is a readiness to forgive, highlighting forgiveness as a settled quality that a person may possess or express. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the verse text.

This Greek LXX verb means to recount or consider—to review something thoughtfully, taking its details into account. It can describe mentally going over what has happened or weighing something carefully before reaching a conclusion. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Isaiah and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is deliberate reflection rather than a quick or careless thought.

This adjective describes something unexpected because it was not hoped for or looked for. It points to an outcome, event, or condition that people did not anticipate or expect. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears once, in Isaiah 18:2. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains clear: something unforeseen, especially because no hope or expectation was directed toward it.

This Greek LXX noun means “axle”: the rod on which a wheel turns. It names a physical part of a vehicle, cart, or similar wheeled object rather than an action or quality. The word occurs six times in the LXX corpus, including passages in Exodus, Proverbs, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains concrete and straightforward; the surrounding verse determines how the axle functions in a particular scene.

This noun means “brilliance,” referring to a shining or radiant quality. It names brightness as something that can be recognized or described, rather than expressing an action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:26. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context; its central lexical idea remains brilliance.

This noun means “simplicity,” describing a quality or condition of being simple. It can name simplicity as a personal or characteristic quality rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX entity, the word occurs seven times across seven verses. Its occurrences include both Old Testament books and deuterocanonical writings, so it is used across more than one literary setting while retaining the same central meaning. The surrounding verse determines how this quality functions in each particular passage.

This verb means to cease speaking or to maintain silence. It describes the stopping of spoken words rather than naming a person, object, or teaching. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 45:27, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. The word’s central idea remains clear: speech comes to an end, and silence is maintained. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the actual sentence in which it appears.

Araba, also rendered Arava, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a named place or region in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings. The name occurs 14 times in this LXX corpus, especially in Deuteronomy and Joshua. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense is the name “Araba” or “Arava,” not an abstract quality or action.

Arim is a proper name used for a place or location in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea, but as the name “Arim.” It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Joshua 19:38 and once in 1 Chronicles 2:51. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s precise geographical or contextual significance cannot be explained further from this record alone.

This noun means “collateral”: something given or held as security to guarantee an agreement or promised action. It refers to a tangible pledge connected with an obligation, rather than to the obligation itself. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs three times, all in Genesis 38, so its recorded use is limited to that passage and does not by itself establish a wider range of meanings. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding text.

This verb means to be “faithless to” someone or something—to fail to remain loyal or faithful. It describes a person’s unfaithful action rather than naming an object, place, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, all in seven Old Testament verses, including passages in Ezra, Nehemiah, and Psalms. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is the breaking of faithfulness.

Achisaar is a personal name, also rendered as Akhisaar. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:10. It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. The available information identifies the person by name but does not provide a separate meaning or description for the name itself. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Basan, also called Vasan, is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament. It refers to a named place or region rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 38 times across 34 verses in the LXX, with many occurrences in Deuteronomy and additional occurrences in Numbers, Joshua, 1 Chronicles, Psalms, and Jeremiah. Its repeated use identifies Basan consistently as a recognized geographical name in the biblical narrative.

This noun means “that which is fed”: something provided with nourishment or food. It names the thing being fed rather than the act of feeding, so its basic focus is on a nourished subject. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, mostly in Old Testament passages. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse, which is needed to identify the subject more specifically.

Galemeth is a proper name, referring to a person named Galemeth in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a description, action, or general spiritual term, but as an identifying name. The name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles: 1 Chronicles 6:45 and 1 Chronicles 9:42. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the person’s specific role and significance cannot be explained from the name alone.

Gallim is a proper name, preserved in English as “Gallim.” It does not function as a general description or action word; it identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This word appears only once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Isaiah 10:30. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its specific contextual significance cannot be explained beyond recognizing Gallim as the name used in that passage.

Gelōrai, also rendered “Yelore,” is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it appears once, at 2 Samuel 23:37. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not state whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the surrounding verse and passage, while its basic function is to designate a particular name in the text.

This word means “scholar,” referring to a learned person, especially someone entrusted with knowledge or official responsibilities. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings to identify people whose learning gives them a recognized place among leaders or administrators. The word occurs 80 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it describes a recurring role rather than a single individual or event.

This Greek LXX adverb means “terribly,” expressing something done or experienced in an intensely severe or alarming way. As an adverb, it modifies an action or description rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Job, Wisdom, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the action or condition it modifies, but its central sense consistently adds strong intensity and seriousness.

This Greek LXX verb means “bind; tie”: to fasten something, hold it together, or restrain it by tying. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its precise force depends on what is being bound and the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 88 times, showing that it is a regularly used word for fastening or tying. Its occurrences span Genesis through Song of Songs.

Diakopē, also written Thiakopi, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a specific name in the Greek Old Testament and appears ten times across seven verses. Because the available lexical definition identifies it only by these name forms, its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding passage in each occurrence, rather than by adding an unsupported meaning. It occurs from Judges through Micah in the LXX corpus.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “disposition” or “arrangement”: the way people, things, or matters are ordered or set in place. It can describe an established order rather than a temporary action. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages connected with the organization of worship and the ordering of sacred spaces. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being arranged and the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes someone or something that is two years old. It gives an age, rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 10:3. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning is straightforward: the person or thing described has reached two years of age.

Dōmana, also rendered “Thomana,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or relationship. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available information does not specify whether the name refers to a person, place, or another designation. This name occurs once, in Judges 1:30. Its exact reference depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut in; carve,” describing the act of making marks or shaping a surface by cutting into it. It is a concrete action word rather than a general term for writing or forming. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, in Job and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and what object is being marked or shaped.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Ezerēl” or “Ezeril.” It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:41. Because the available wording gives only the name and no verse text, its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

This verb means “winnow” or “sift”—to separate useful grain from what is unwanted. It describes an act of sorting or cleansing by removing what does not belong. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 5:23. The word therefore presents separation as an active process, whether referring to grain or using that familiar action as a picture of decisive removal. Its exact force in Wisdom 5:23 is determined by the surrounding verse and passage.

Ellasar is a proper name used to identify someone or something called Ellasar. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears twice, both times in Genesis 14—once in Genesis 14:1 and again in Genesis 14:9. The available meaning is simply the name “Ellasar”; the word itself does not provide an additional descriptive meaning. Its precise significance in either passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective means “in the fire.” It describes something associated with, located in, or characterized by fire, functioning as a descriptive word rather than naming the fire itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Ezekiel and Amos. Its basic sense remains concise: it identifies a person or thing in relation to fire. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “tame”: to bring something under control rather than leave it wild or unrestrained. It describes an action, so it refers to the act of taming, not simply to something already gentle. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 4 Maccabees 1:29. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the bringing of a person, animal, or force into a controlled state.

gl: buoy up with hope; cheat with false hopes
d: buoy up with hope; cheat with false hopes

e.t: This Greek LXX verb describes giving someone hopeful encouragement, or misleading them by raising false hopes. Its central idea is hope presented to a person, whether that hope truly supports them or deceptively lifts their expectations. It occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, especially in the Psalms. Because it is a verb, it expresses an action: someone is being buoyed up with hope or being cheated through false hopes. The surrounding verse determines which sense is active.

This Greek LXX verb expresses being “in need of” something or “fasten on” something. As a verb, it can describe a need that calls for help or attachment to another thing, depending on the sentence. It occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic idea is repeated across several biblical settings. The surrounding words determine whether the emphasis is need or fastening.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a superintendent or chief—someone placed in charge of people, work, or responsibilities. It describes a recognized leader or overseer rather than an ordinary worker. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, including passages connected with labor supervision, administration, and officials. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains one who directs or oversees others.

This adverb means “from the other side.” It describes where something comes from or the direction from which it approaches, marking a position opposite or across from another place. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:4. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic idea is movement or origin from the opposite side.

This LXX word means “till” or “until.” It marks the endpoint of a period, action, or condition, telling the reader how long something continues or when a change is reached. It can function in a sentence as a conjunction, preposition, adverb, or noun, depending on its use. The word occurs 1,356 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing throughout the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding words and the event or time being described.

This verb means “yoke together”: to join two things under one yoke or connect them for shared work. It describes bringing things into a paired arrangement rather than keeping them separate. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 1 Kings and once in Ezekiel. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but its central idea remains joining together under a common yoke or connection.

This Greek LXX noun means “life” or “vitality”—the living principle or condition that distinguishes a living being from what is dead. It can refer broadly to life itself, including the life possessed by people and other living creatures. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 253 times across 241 verses, from Genesis through 4 Maccabees. Its ordinary meaning remains centered on being alive and possessing life, while the surrounding passage determines the particular aspect being discussed.

Thau is the name of a Hebrew alphabet letter. It functions as a noun, identifying the letter rather than describing an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, at Psalm 118:169. Because the available information gives the letter’s name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise role in that line cannot be explained further here. The word itself is a designation: Thau.

This Greek LXX verb means to die or to depart from life. It describes the end of a person's earthly life and can also describe someone who has already died. The word appears 89 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, showing that it is a normal term for death rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “doorkeeper”: a person assigned to watch or attend a doorway. It identifies someone whose responsibility is connected with a door, such as controlling access, guarding an entrance, or serving those who pass through. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, and Ezekiel. The word itself names the person and does not, by itself, describe whether the duty is temporary, official, voluntary, or connected with a particular building.

Iamoun, also given as Iamun, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Numbers 26:17. Because the available information does not include the verse text or surrounding context, the name itself does not establish further details about the person, place, family, or event connected with it.

“Priesthood” refers to the priestly office or body of priests—the people appointed to serve God in a priestly capacity. It is a noun describing this sacred role or community rather than one individual priest. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs three times: twice in Exodus and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains the priesthood itself.

Itaburion is a place-name, also rendered Tabor. It identifies the same named location in the Greek Old Testament and is not a description of a quality, action, or person. The word occurs twice in the LXX corpus, once in Jeremiah 26:18 and once in Hosea 5:1. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise role in either passage cannot be explained further, but its basic meaning remains the name Itaburion, or Tabor.

This adjective describes someone who is ill-disposed—inclined toward harmful or hostile intentions—or malicious. It portrays a person’s character or attitude as actively unfriendly rather than merely mistaken, weak, or unfortunate. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a deliberately bad or harmful disposition toward others.

This Greek LXX noun means an “inroad” or “raid”—a sudden incursion into a place or territory. It refers to an act of entering hostilely, usually with the sense of attack or military aggression. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 5:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This verb means “establish”: to set something in place or make it firm. It describes the act of giving something a settled position rather than merely mentioning or observing it. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Job 20:7, so its broader range of use cannot be traced through many passages. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and context, but its central idea is establishing something securely or decisively.

This Greek LXX verb means “settle”: to cause people to take up residence in a place. It can describe establishing someone in a land or dwelling, rather than merely visiting it. The word occurs 33 times in the LXX corpus, so it expresses a recurring action of placing or establishing inhabitants. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “break”: to cause something to separate, crack, or lose its wholeness. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so the surrounding sentence identifies what is being broken. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Judges, Jeremiah, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what the sentence says is broken.

This adjective means “common; vulgar,” describing something ordinary, shared, or belonging to people generally rather than being set apart as special. It can refer to what is commonplace or broadly held in common. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs 24 times, so it has a recurring role in describing ordinary or shared things. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This adjective describes something made with tassels or hanging fringe along its edge. It points to a visible decorative feature rather than an action or inner quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs three times, including two occurrences in Exodus and one in Psalms. Its basic sense is therefore physical and descriptive: something is tasselled, fringed, or finished with ornamental threads. The surrounding passage determines what object carries this feature in each occurrence.

This adjective means “of cypress-wood,” describing something made from or associated with cypress wood. It identifies the material or kind of wood being mentioned rather than expressing an action or quality such as strength or beauty. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Nehemiah 8:15 and Ezekiel 27:24. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains a reference to cypress wood.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Labiim” and also identified as “Lavim.” It functions as a name rather than a descriptive word or action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Genesis 10:13. Since the available wording supplies the name but not the surrounding verse text, its broader identity or role must be understood from that passage rather than added to the name itself.

This word means “lion,” the large, powerful wild animal. It is a noun used for lions as actual creatures and may also serve in descriptions or comparisons involving their strength, danger, or imposing presence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 140 times, so it is a well-established word across that corpus rather than a rare or specialized term. Its earliest listed occurrence is Genesis 49:9, and its latest is Song of Songs 4:8. The precise force of the word in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “wolf,” the name of a wild animal. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings. The word appears nine times in this LXX corpus, with occurrences spanning Genesis, Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Habakkuk, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains the animal itself.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Maachati” or “Maakhati.” It functions as a name rather than a descriptive term or action word. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 23:34. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide further meaning or contextual detail, so it is best understood simply as the personal or identifying name represented by these two renderings.

This word means “long-lived”. It describes someone or something characterized by an extended length of life. As an adjective, it adds this quality to a person or thing rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Isaiah and once in Wisdom. Its basic sense remains focused on duration of life, while the surrounding passage determines what person or thing is being described. The word is rendered “long-lived” in the available English translation support.

Manathi is a personal name, referring to someone identified by that name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles. Because the available wording gives only the name itself and no descriptive definition, its ordinary meaning is simply the personal designation “Manathi.” The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain which person is meant in either occurrence.

Mebaar, also rendered Mevaar, is a proper name. It functions as a name rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:38. The available information identifies the name and its location, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whether it names a person, place, or another specific subject in that passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “apple” or “fruit,” referring to a kind of produce. It names an actual food and can be used wherever the surrounding passage identifies or compares something with such produce. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament, across Genesis, Proverbs, Joel, and Song of Songs. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on the surrounding text, but its basic meaning remains a fruit, specifically an apple or similar fruit.

Nekōda, also written Nekotha, is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person or family designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs four times in the Greek LXX, appearing twice in Ezra and twice in Nehemiah. Its occurrences are in Ezra 2:48, Ezra 2:60, Nehemiah 7:50, and Nehemiah 7:62. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify precisely whom the name designates in each passage.

Noema is a proper name, referring to a person named Noema. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Genesis 4:22. The name itself is given as “Noema”; the available information does not provide an additional descriptive meaning or explain the person’s role. Therefore, its normal function is simply to identify this individual within the genealogy and narrative of Genesis, rather than to express an action, quality, or theological concept.

This adjective means “eight cubits long,” describing the measured length of something. A cubit was an ancient unit of length, so the word identifies an object by its stated measurement rather than describing a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Kings 7:47. Its precise referent and significance depend on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is a length measuring eight cubits.

This Greek LXX adjective means “broiled,” describing food prepared by direct heat. It identifies something as cooked in that manner rather than naming a person, place, or action. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Exodus 12:8–9. Its ordinary meaning is therefore straightforward: it describes food that has been broiled. The precise force in either verse comes from the surrounding wording, but the word itself points specifically to the method of cooking.

This word means “who” or “what,” pointing to a person, thing, or matter being identified or asked about. It functions as a pronoun and can refer back to someone or something already mentioned, or introduce a question about identity. In the Greek Old Testament, it is very common, occurring 8,094 times, so its exact force depends on whether the sentence is identifying, describing, or asking. Its basic meaning remains focused on identifying a person or thing.

The word means “master gardener,” referring to a person responsible for overseeing and directing garden work. As a noun, it identifies that kind of worker rather than describing an action or quality. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 1:29. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular role there; the basic meaning remains a master gardener.

This adjective describes someone as “crafty”—acting with calculated skill or cleverness rather than straightforward openness. It characterizes a person or their conduct, so its force depends on the surrounding sentence and whether the action is being praised or exposed. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs 19 times, with most occurrences in Proverbs. Its central idea remains a person who uses craft or clever methods in dealing with others.

This noun means “convoying”: accompanying someone or something as an escort while traveling. It describes the act of going along with another party, generally to provide accompaniment or protection during a journey. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 9:37. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the specific situation cannot be described further; the word’s basic sense is the act of convoying.

This verb means to infiltrate—to enter quietly or secretly into a place or group. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so it normally tells what someone does when gaining entry without being openly noticed. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 8:1. The verse’s precise force depends on its surrounding wording, which is not included here; the basic sense remains secret entry.

This Greek LXX verb means “stand by” or be “present.” It describes someone positioning themselves nearby, appearing before another person, or being available to serve or act. The word is used 82 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense covers both physical standing and being present in a situation. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains being there or standing ready before someone.

This verb describes something that “flow[s] round,” moving around or encircling a person, object, or place. It focuses on the motion of flowing as it passes around its surrounding subject. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 9:20. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and does not need to be expanded beyond this basic picture of circular or encompassing flow.

This Greek LXX noun means “breath,” the air or life-breath associated with living beings. It can describe the breath that comes from a person or creature and, in some passages, the life-giving breath God gives. The word occurs 23 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, from Genesis through 2 Maccabees. Its ordinary sense remains focused on breath as a sign and expression of life.

“Gone over; passed” describes something that has already moved across or gone by. As an adjective, the word characterizes a person or thing in terms of having passed from one place or point to another, or having gone by. Its exact force in a sentence depends on what is described, but its central idea is completed passage or movement onward. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, in Esther and 2 Maccabees.

This Greek LXX verb means to set something up as a pretext—that is, to present a stated reason that serves as a cover or excuse for another purpose. It describes the act of using an outward explanation to conceal or justify what one really intends. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once each in 2 Kings, Psalms, and Proverbs. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Remmōna, also rendered Rhemmona, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or location in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 19:13. The available lexical information preserves the name itself, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain its specific role in that passage.

Romelias is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used as the name Romelias, also rendered Rhomelias. The name occurs 12 times in 12 verses, appearing in 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Isaiah. Because personal names identify individuals, its meaning is primarily its identifying use rather than a general idea or definition. The exact person intended in any particular verse must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text.

This noun means “satrap” or “viceroy,” a high-ranking ruler or appointed official within a kingdom. It refers to someone exercising authority on behalf of a greater king or imperial government. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 24 times, showing that it is a recognized title for governing officials rather than a general word for any leader. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding context and the person or group being described.
